name: Recursive Function (Factorial / Fibonacci)
description: Stack frame allocation via alloca, absence of TCO in Flang, call graph in FIR, phi nodes for conditional result selection
source:
recursive function factorial(n) result(r)
  integer, intent(in) :: n
  integer(kind=8)     :: r
  if (n <= 1) then
    r = 1
  else
    r = n * factorial(n - 1)
  end if
end function factorial

semantics.content:
Symbol table: factorial
  n:  INTEGER(4) intent=IntentIn  rank=0
  r:  INTEGER(8) local (result variable)  rank=0
  factorial: FunctionEntityDetails  RECURSIVE  result=r

Recursion analysis:
  Self-call: factorial(n-1)
    Argument: n-1 (scalar expression, no aliasing with dummy n)
    Result: INTEGER(8) — same as r
  Tail call? NO — result is used in multiplication: r = n * factorial(n-1)
    Therefore TCO is NOT applicable; each call allocates a new stack frame
  Stack depth: O(n) — proportional to argument value
  Base case: n <= 1 → r = 1 (no recursive call)
  Flang DOES NOT emit MUSTTAIL or any tail-call optimization attribute
    even if the programmer writes a tail-recursive form

llvm_ir.content:
; ModuleID = '09_recursion.f90'

define i64 @_QPfactorial(ptr nocapture readonly %0) #0 !dbg !5 {
entry:
  ; Each call allocates: n_argument_copy + r_result on stack
  %n_m1_alloca = alloca i32, align 4    ; storage for n-1 argument to recursive call
  %r_alloca    = alloca i64, align 8    ; result variable r

  %n_val = load i32, ptr %0, align 4, !dbg !10
  %cond  = icmp sle i32 %n_val, 1, !dbg !11
  br i1 %cond, label %then_block, label %else_block, !dbg !11

then_block:                             ; n <= 1: r = 1
  store i64 1, ptr %r_alloca, align 8, !dbg !12
  br label %merge

else_block:                             ; r = n * factorial(n-1)
  %n64   = sext i32 %n_val to i64, !dbg !13
  %n_m1  = sub nsw i32 %n_val, 1, !dbg !13
  store i32 %n_m1, ptr %n_m1_alloca, align 4, !dbg !13

  ; Recursive call — note: no 'tail' or 'musttail' attribute
  ; Each call pushes a new stack frame, depth = O(n)
  %recur = call i64 @_QPfactorial(ptr %n_m1_alloca), !dbg !13

  %prod  = mul nsw i64 %n64, %recur, !dbg !13
  store i64 %prod, ptr %r_alloca, align 8, !dbg !13
  br label %merge

merge:                                  ; phi to unify then/else paths
  %r_val = load i64, ptr %r_alloca, align 8, !dbg !14
  ret i64 %r_val, !dbg !14
}

; WHY NO TAIL CALL OPTIMIZATION:
; The recursive call 'factorial(n-1)' appears as the RHS of a multiply:
;   r = n * factorial(n-1)
; This means the call result must be held in a register while 'n' is
; also live. The current frame cannot be reused — TCO is illegal.
; Even if written as a tail-recursive helper, Flang does not implement
; Fortran-level TCO (unlike GCC's -foptimize-sibling-calls).

!5  = distinct !DISubprogram(name: "factorial", line: 10)
!10 = !DILocation(line: 11, column: 3, scope: !5)
!11 = !DILocation(line: 13, column: 3, scope: !5)
!12 = !DILocation(line: 14, column: 5, scope: !5)
!13 = !DILocation(line: 16, column: 5, scope: !5)
!14 = !DILocation(line: 18, column: 1, scope: !5)

correlations.lowering_notes: The recursive call to factorial(n-1) cannot be tail-call optimized because its result is immediately consumed in a multiply instruction (n * result). Flang emits a standard call without 'tail' or 'musttail' annotation. Each invocation allocates two stack slots: one for the n-1 argument copy (required since Flang passes by reference) and one for the result variable r. Stack depth grows linearly with n.

The IF construct lowers to fir.if in FIR (a structured two-region operation), then to an LLVM conditional branch. The 'merge' basic block at the end is not a phi node — instead both paths write to the stack-allocated %r_alloca then fall into the merge block for a load. This is a consequence of using an explicit result variable rather than SSA form.

lowering_patterns.name: Recursive Call: No TCO in Flang
lowering_patterns.description: Flang does not implement tail-call optimization. Every recursive call emits a standard LLVM call (not musttail), and each frame allocates stack space for the result variable and any argument temporaries

lowering_patterns.name: Fortran Pass-by-Reference for Scalars
lowering_patterns.description: Scalar arguments are passed as pointers (ptr/!fir.ref<i32>) per Fortran ABI. Recursive calls must allocate a fresh stack slot for each by-ref argument, contributing to the per-frame stack cost
